clinicalPearls: Pain arising from the sacroiliac joint, typically felt over the buttock and posterior superior iliac spine and sometimes referring to the groin or posterior thigh
The Fortin finger test, in which the patient points to pain just inferomedial to the posterior superior iliac spine, is characteristic
No single examination test is diagnostic, and a cluster of provocation tests improves accuracy
Provocation tests include FABER (Patrick), thigh thrust, compression, distraction (gapping), and Gaenslen manoeuvres
A commonly used rule is that three or more positive provocation tests raise the likelihood of a sacroiliac source
Pain often worsens with transitional movements, prolonged sitting or standing, and climbing stairs
An image-guided intra-articular anaesthetic block is the reference standard for diagnosis
Management is largely conservative (physiotherapy, pelvic stabilisation, analgesia), with image-guided injection and, rarely, joint fusion for refractory cases
reference.pathophysiology: Sacroiliac joint dysfunction encompasses pain generated by the sacroiliac joint, a large, partly synovial joint that transmits load between the spine and pelvis and is stabilised by strong ligaments. Pain may result from altered joint mechanics (hypermobility or hypomobility), ligamentous strain, degenerative change, pregnancy-related laxity, leg-length discrepancy, or previous lumbar fusion increasing adjacent load. The joint and its ligaments are innervated by branches from the dorsal rami, and both intra-articular and extra-articular (ligamentous) sources can contribute to the pain.
additionalDifferentials: Lumbar facet joint or discogenic pain
additionalInvestigations: A cluster of provocation tests (thigh thrust, compression, distraction, FABER, Gaenslen)
Image-guided intra-articular anaesthetic block as the reference standard
MRI of the sacroiliac joints to exclude inflammatory sacroiliitis (bone marrow oedema)
Plain radiographs of the pelvis and hips to assess degenerative or structural change
Inflammatory markers and HLA-B27 if spondyloarthropathy is suspected
redFlags: Inflammatory features (young patient, morning stiffness, alternating buttock pain, good response to anti-inflammatories) suggesting axial spondyloarthritis
Constitutional symptoms suggesting infection or malignancy
reference.prognosis: Most cases improve with conservative treatment and correction of contributing factors; image-guided injections often give useful relief, and outcomes are generally favourable, although a minority have persistent pain.
pitfalls: Missing inflammatory sacroiliitis by not considering axial spondyloarthritis
Relying on a single provocation test rather than a cluster
Overlooking hip pathology presenting as buttock or groin pain
references: Laslett: Evidence-based diagnosis and treatment of the painful sacroiliac joint
management: Structured physiotherapy targeting lumbopelvic and core stabilisation, with correction of contributing factors such as leg-length discrepancy
Simple analgesia and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for symptomatic pain relief
Image-guided intra-articular corticosteroid and local anaesthetic injection for both diagnostic confirmation and therapeutic relief
Radiofrequency ablation of the lateral branch sensory nerves for refractory pain confirmed to arise from the joint
Pelvic girdle support and activity modification for pregnancy-related laxity and transitional-movement pain
Sacroiliac joint arthrodesis or minimally invasive fusion reserved for disabling pain unresponsive to conservative measures
Referral to a spinal or pain specialist when structured conservative treatment fails
